notes: "For a long time, no man fell." reads slightly stiff; "For a long time, nobody fell." is more natural and still A1.
The bow/coward exchange is dropped at A1; this is acceptable condensing, since the big man simply invites Robin to get a staff.
Possible A1 lookups (by myself, blew, toward) are few and inferable from context; not a comprehension blocker.
"Two men could not pass on it." -> "Two men could not pass each other on it." is more idiomatic.
"Now we are the same," said Robin. -> "Now it is fair," said Robin. would sound more natural.
"Do you want me to show you?" is slightly elliptical (show what?); "Do you want me to show you who is better?" would be clearer. Understandable from context.
"Nobody ever called him a coward" -> "Nobody had ever called him a coward" reads more naturally (past perfect is allowed at B1).

Robin is "sitting in the water up to his chest" yet says "I am floating down with the current"; this is his joke from the original and works, but "standing in the water" or dropping the chest detail would avoid a small literal clash.
"looked at him with mild disgust" -> "looked at him with quiet scorn" fits the tone better.

Faithful to Pyle's account: log bridge, "better man" exchange, arrow threat and coward charge, six-foot oak staff, fall into the stream with the "floating with the current" reply, three horn blasts, Will Stutely, three suits of Lincoln green, renaming by Will Stutely, and the feast. Ale is omitted, which suits the 4+ rating.
The rib blow is stated without any injury detail, so it is acceptable for 4+.

summary: All five levels retell Pyle's episode faithfully, keep events and names consistent across levels, respect the grammar limits for each level, and stay within 4+ suitability; every quiz has a single correct, defensible key. The only remaining points are minor phrasing preferences, listed as notes.
